region.en: Kingdom of Nepal, by the King's palace (symbolic pin at Kathmandu)
region.zh: 尼泊爾王國王宮附近（以加德滿都為象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XII

summary.en: A Mouse prays for a strong child and bears a Tiger, for a beautiful child a Peacock, and for a wise, wealthy and powerful child a man-child whose hair turns to diamonds and whose nail-parings to turquoises. A greedy King, tipped off by a barber, tries to enslave the Boy with impossible demands - four Tigers for the gates, four Peacocks for the golden pinnacles, and finally that the Mouse herself fight the state Elephant - but the handfuls of hair and feathers summon a hundred Tigers and a sky full of Peacocks, and the poisoned Mouse runs up the Elephant's trunk into its brain and kills it. The King keeps his word: the daughter, half the kingdom, and in time the throne.
summary.zh: 母鼠求子：求強得虎、求美得孔雀、求智富權得人子——其髮落地成鑽石珍珠、指甲成綠松石。貪婪的國王聽理髮匠之言，連出難題——四虎守四門、四孔雀棲四金頂、母鼠單挑御象——但一把虎毛召來百虎，一把雀羽引來滿天孔雀；鼠抹毒鑽入象鼻直上象腦，毒斃巨獸。國王踐諾：嫁女、分半國，後傳位於他。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as heritage of the Nepal-Tibet storytelling borderlands.

passages.text: Praying that her offspring might be very strong, the Mouse bore a young Tiger, who left her a handful of his hair: go into yonder thicket, throw it into the air and call my name three times. The beautiful child was a Peacock, who left feathers with the same instruction; and the third child, prayed to become wise, wealthy and powerful, was a man-child.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: A barber cutting the Boy's hair saw each hair fall as diamonds and pearls and each nail-paring as turquoises, and told the greedy King, who demanded four full-grown Tigers for the palace gates under threat of killing the mother; a handful of Tiger's hair summoned a great Tiger who opened his mouth with fearful roars until the whole jungle was full of hastening Tigers, and the Boy rode one's back to the throne. The Peacocks came the same way, four carrying the Boy to the King's courtyard, tails spread in rows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: For the third trial the King demanded that Mother Mouse single-handed fight and destroy the state Elephant; she had herself smeared with poison and a long string tied to her tail, and carried in the Boy's sleeve. As the chained Elephant rushed bellowing, the Mouse hopped onto his foot and scuttled up the trunk into his brain, running round and round smearing poison; the Elephant fell stone dead, and the Boy, pulling the string, guided her out into the open air. The King gave him his daughter in marriage and half his kingdom, and on the King's death the Boy succeeded to the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: Thickest part of a Tibetan forest (symbolic pin in southeastern Tibet)
region.zh: 藏東南密林深處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XIII

summary.en: Driven from a village by too many dogs, a family of Jackals squats in a Tiger's den while he hunts. Father Jackal stations himself on the roof and raps a stone when the Tiger approaches, so that Mrs. Jackal can set the children crying for their supper of hot Tiger's meat; the terrified Tiger flees. An old Baboon laughs at him - you should eat the Jackals, not the Jackals you - and walks back with him, tail twisted round the Tiger's for support; but at the cry 'Brother Monkey, bring him along quickly - only one?' the Tiger bolts for good, dragging the Baboon through the thorns until only a broken bit of tail remains twisted round the Tiger's own.
summary.zh: 豺一家被村犬逼走，霸佔了虎穴。父豺守在穴頂，見虎歸來便敲石示意；母豺讓孩子們大哭「等虎肉晚餐」。虎嚇破膽逃走，遇白鬚老狒狒譏笑「該是你吃豺，不是豺吃你」，尾纏虎尾同行壯膽；穴頂一聲「猴兄，快帶他來——怎麼只帶一個？」，虎掉頭狂奔，把狒狒拖過荊棘叢，最後虎尾上只纏著一截斷落的猴尾。豺從此安居虎穴。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: Father Jackal arranged the stratagem: rapping with a loose stone on the roof of the den as the Tiger approached, he called out what are those children crying about, and was answered that they were very hungry and impatient for their supper; tell them they won't have long to wait now, he replied, the Tiger will probably be home very soon and we shall all be eating hot Tiger's meat before long. The Tiger thought what kind of strange animal can this be which has entered my den and is waiting to cook and eat me on my return - and turned tail and ran off through the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: An old Baboon with a fringe of white hair round his face laughed heartily: you should eat the Jackals, and not the Jackals you; come along with me and I will show you how to deal with people like that. Twisting his tail round the Tiger's to give him confidence, the Baboon walked with him toward the den - until Father Jackal called out, that is right, Brother Monkey, bring him along quickly; we are all half starved - but what do you mean by only bringing one of them? The Tiger fled precipitately, dragging the Baboon through the thickest and thorniest parts of the jungle until many miles away all he saw of the Monkey was a bit of its tail broken off and still twisted round his own.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Thieves at the Court of the Emperor

region.en: Palace court of the Emperor of China (symbolic pin at Beijing)
region.zh: 中國皇帝宮廷（以北京為象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XIV

summary.en: Three master-thieves meet at an inn - one can lift eggs from under a sitting hen, one can cut the soles off a walking man's boots, one can eat his fill off a man's plate unseen - and enter the Emperor's service by undoing, at a single audience, three scandals their own night's work created: the vanished peahen's eggs, the soleless Prime Minister imprisoned for a breach of etiquette, and the starving Emperor. For a final test the Emperor demands three Treasury pearls by next evening - and the thieves simply join the huge inventory party in official robes, each pocketing a pearl already entered on the list.
summary.zh: 三個絕技神偷在客棧相識——掏孵蛋母雞之卵、割行人之靴底、就席偷食他人盤中餐——為揚名於中國皇帝，各自「作案」：偷走御雉蛋、剝去宰相靴底、吃光御膳，再在公開召見時「物歸原主」救出被囚的宰相與御廚。皇帝最後一試：明晚六時前取出三顆內庫珍珠——他們只須混入清點寶庫的數百官員之中，點入清單後各藏一顆便大功告成。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as heritage of the Tibet-China storytelling borderlands.

passages.text: The first Thief had lifted the Emperor's pea-hen's eggs from under the sitting hen without her knowing; the second had cut the soles off the Prime Minister's new boots, so that when he knelt to kow-tow the Emperor, thinking the breach deliberate, imprisoned him for beheading unless the soles were produced; the third had taken the food from each dish as it was placed on the table until the Emperor, unable to make a satisfactory meal, had ordered the whole of his Cooks and Chamberlains imprisoned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: At the public audience the three produced eggs, soles and dinner-plate in turn; the Emperor laughed heartily, released the Prime Minister and all the domestic officials, and then, before rewarding them, set a further test: three of the pearls from his Treasury, enclosed within a treble wall ten fathoms high and guarded by companies of soldiers, must be produced by six o'clock next evening, or the three should be put to death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Thieves suggested a complete enumeration of the Treasury first, so the pearls could be proved missing; and when hundreds of palace officials were called in to inventory it section by section, the three, dressed in the complete robes proper for a palace official, mingled unnoticed in the crowd, were allotted sections, and each, after first placing a large pearl upon his list, secreted it. At six o'clock next day they laid three pearls on the steps of the throne; the Treasurer found three pearls missing, and the Emperor raised the Thieves to high rank with lands and money.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Boy with the Deformed Head and the Fairy Bride

region.en: Small lake in a herding valley (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XV

summary.en: A cowherd boy born with a head deformed fore and aft watches a great white Drake circle the lake daily, catches him in a yaks'-hair rope-and-loop ring, and rejects his gold for the middle of his three daughters - for nine years only. The fairy wife raises a palace from magic, but on the last morning of the ninth year the Boy wakes on a bleak hillside with nothing but memory. Wandering, he saves three young Gryphons from a Dragon, and the grateful Gryphon carries him up through the golden gates to plead his case before the assembly of the gods - where the fairy bride rushes into his arms, the conclave consents, and she becomes mortal to return with him, the two living to a good old age.
summary.zh: 牛倌少年天生頭部前後突出、面貌醜陋。他日日觀看白鴨繞湖三匝，以犛牛毛繩圈套住牠；不要金銀珠寶，只求仙女的三女兒中的二女兒為妻——限九年。仙妻以法術建起華美宮殿，然而第九年最後一夜醒來，一切都消失了，只餘記憶。流浪途中他斬殺欲吞三隻幼獅鷲的巨龍；感恩的獅鷲馱他穿過金門直上神國，眾神震怒之際仙女新娘撲入他懷中；神議決定放行，但嫁凡人者須失去仙性。她欣然應允，二人重返人間白頭偕老。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Boy wove a long rope of yaks' hair big enough to encircle the lake, with fine horsehair loops floating in the water; the Drake, caught, revealed himself a fairy King who descended daily to amuse himself by swimming round and round, and offered gold, silver, jewels and coral. The Boy laughed: I do not care at all for your gold or your jewels, but what I really want is a wife - and chose the middle of the three daughters, accepting the condition that a fairy can live with a mortal only nine years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The fairy wife erected a magnificent palace by her magic and furnished it luxuriously; but when the nine years ended the young Man awoke on a bleak hillside near the spot where he had first conversed with the Fairy King - his palace, his servants, his horses and, worst of all, his beautiful wife had all disappeared utterly, and nothing remained but a memory.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Half distracted he wandered until he found three young Gryphons terrorized by an immense Dragon crossing the lake to devour them; drawing his sword he engaged the monster single-handed and severed its head from its neck. The grateful parent Gryphons carried him through the great golden gates to the country of the gods, where the assembly rose in wrath at the introduction of a human being - and where the fairy bride, hiding till then, rushed forward and threw herself into her husband's arms. The conclave decided that as she desired to return of her own free will she must take the consequence and become mortal; she joyfully agreed, and the two were deposited near their old home, where they grew to a good old age.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince and the Ogre's Castle

region.en: Ogre's castle in a valley below a high pass (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 啞口之下谷中的魔堡（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XVI

summary.en: A childless King buys nine pills from a Lama who is really a man-eating Ogre: three children, three foals and three pups are born, and after three years the Ogre claims the youngest of each. At the castle the boy-Prince performs the first tasks unafraid - a bundle of straw turns to wolves devouring the goat, soaked grain to wild cats destroying the fowls - and finds in a glass room a Princess who sleeps under an enchanted flower: the Ogre eats men's hearts and gains power only over servants who disobey, while his own life depends on a hidden mascot. She coaches the counter-tricks: ask the Ogre to lead the way round the stove in the dark, then ask him to demonstrate the kow-tow - and when his face touches the ground the third time, the Prince's sword takes his head. In the vaults the mascot is a beautiful boy with a goblet of crystal liquid, each drop a man's life; the victims' hearts eaten, one drop each restores the scores of bodies in the back chamber.
summary.zh: 無子的國王從假扮喇嘛的食人魔處求得九丸仙藥：王后、母馬、母犬各生三子；三年後魔依約索走最年幼的三者。少年王子在魔堡不為怪事所懼——草束化三狼食羊、濕糧化三野貓盡毀雞群——並在玻璃室喚醒被魔花催眠的公主。公主道破魔的規則：只有僕人抗命他才能吃其心；其命則繫於密藏的「命石」。她教王子以計反制：請魔先行繞灶、請魔示範磕頭——魔額第三次觸地時，王子揮劍斬首。地窖深處「命石」乃一美童手捧水晶杯，杯中滴滴皆人命；以一滴復一人，後屋數十具無心之身盡數甦醒。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Ogre, disguised as a holy Lama, gave the King nine pills - three for the Queen, three for the mare, three for the dog - and after three months a child was born to each, followed by two others at intervals of one month; at the end of three years the Ogre returned to demand the youngest son, the youngest horse and the youngest dog.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The tasks the Ogre set grew stranger: a bundle of straw became three great wolves who devoured the goat and fled, and a handful of soaked grain became three wild cats who destroyed the fowls. The Prince pushed open the castle door and found in a glass room a beautiful lady asleep with a flower behind her ear; taking away the flower woke her, and she explained that the Lama was a wicked Ogre who partakes of nothing but men's hearts, and gains power over a human being only when that being directly disobeys his orders.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Ordered to walk three times round the great stove in the dark kitchen, the Prince asked the Ogre to precede and show him the way; ordered to kow-tow three times, the Prince asked to be taught, and as the Ogre's face touched the ground the third time he delivered a violent blow and severed the Ogre's head from his body. The mascot - the beautiful boy in the ninth subterranean chamber with a goblet of crystal liquid, each drop a man's life - was slain, and one drop sprinkled on each of the scores of bodies in the back chamber restored the Ogre's victims, who thanked the Prince and Princess and returned to their own homes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Stone Lion of the Hillside

region.en: Wooded hillside by a well-cultivated valley (symbolic pin in the Nyang valley)
region.zh: 年楚河谷旁山林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XVII

summary.en: Turned out by his clever, selfish elder brother, the dull younger son and his mother settle in a hillside hut; he chops wood, and finding a life-sized Lion carved in stone takes it for the mountain's guardian deity and lights candles to it. The Lion speaks and vomits a bucketful of gold with the warning that no single piece must fall to the ground; mother and son grow rich. The elder brother demands the secret, buys the largest bucket, and shakes the gold down until a piece slips off - the stream stops, the largest piece sticks in the Lion's throat, and the jaws close on his arm. Only when his wife, sold down to the last scrap, comes weeping that they must all starve does the Lion laugh - ha, ha! - and in the open jaws the man wrenches himself free.
summary.zh: 能幹而自私的兄長趕走老實的弟弟；弟弟與母親在山腳茅屋落腳，砍柴度日，遇見山石上刻的等身石獅，供燭參拜。石獅開口，以口吐金，但嚴令「一粒也不可落地」。母子因此致富；兄長聞訊討教，買了全鎮最大的桶，還要把金子搖實多裝——一粒金落地，金流即止，最大一粒卡在獅喉，獅口合攏咬住其臂。直到他妻子變賣殆盡、哭訴「一家都快餓死」，石獅忍俊不禁「哈哈」開口大笑——他趁隙抽臂而逃。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: Finding himself face to face with a large life-sized Lion carved out of the stone, the boy took it for the guardian deity of the mountain, lit two candles before it, and prostrated himself for renewed good fortune. The Lion opened its mouth and asked what he was doing there; told to bring a large bucket, the boy held it under the Lion's mouth and caught a stream of gold pieces, informing the Lion before the bucket was quite full, as on no account must a single morsel of gold fall to the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The elder brother bought the largest bucket to be had and shook the bucket slightly from time to time to make the gold level, so as to obtain a larger quantity; overcome by greed he could not bring himself to warn the Lion until the bucket brimmed over and a piece of gold fell to the ground. The stream ceased, the Lion said hoarsely that the largest piece of all had stuck in his throat and asked him to put his hand in and pull it out - and closed his stone jaws on the arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: His wife brought him food daily while she grew poorer and sold her household goods, until one morning she came weeping up the hill: there is not a scrap left to eat anywhere, and now nothing remains but for us to starve to death. The Lion was so tickled that he could not refrain from laughing - ha, ha! - and opened his great jaws; as quickly as he could, before the Lion had time to close his mouth again, the man withdrew his arm, and the forgiving younger brother eventually supplied him with a small farm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: Lonely hill-top hermitage in Tibet (symbolic pin in the Tsari region)
region.zh: 藏地扎日一帶的孤山修行處（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XVIII

summary.en: The holy Lama's meat-abstaining diet starves his joker of a servant Rin-dzin, who rigs a slip-knot rope through the floor and talks the meditating Lama into 'holding a neighbour's sheep' while he poicks it into strangling itself below; several days of mutton follow, until the shepherd boy witnesses the trick and the Lama dismisses him. On the road Rin-dzin falls in with a thief who plants him behind a fresh corpse and passes himself off as the long-lost son - asking the corpse itself, and getting the sepulchral 'You are' - then decamps with a bag of gold; Rin-dzin overtakes him, drops two boots along the road, and while the thief trudges back for the pair, rides off with the gold.
summary.zh: 持齋的喇嘛讓饞肉的滑頭僕人仁增餓得發慌；仁增把繩圈穿過樓板，哄沉思的喇嘛「替鄰居拴羊」，自己在樓下捅羊致其勒斃，吃了幾天羊肉。放羊娃窺破告發，喇嘛將他逐出。路上他遇一賊，二人合謀：仁增藏於新亡人之柩旁扮鬼，賊冒認失散多年的「弟弟」，向屍體問話得到陰森的「你是」——騙走一大袋金子。仁增借馬追趕，沿路丟下兩隻新靴；賊為撿成一雙回頭取靴，仁增便馱金而走。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Servant caught a strayed sheep, hitched a slip-knot round its neck with a rope let down through a hole in the floor, and asked the meditating Lama to hold the rope while he went to inform the owner - and poked the sheep with a sharp stick below, until the tug-of-war strangled it. When he returned he informed the Lama that the sheep had died a natural death while he was away, and for several days the Servant was able to eat his fill of excellent mutton; but the shepherd boy had seen all that happened through the window, and the Lama, much incensed, dismissed him on the spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Thief's plan was ready-made: the owner of a great house had died awaiting burial, leaving one daughter, a son long lost - so Rin-dzin climbed in by the window and hid near the corpse, and the Thief told the mourning girl he was her long-lost brother and proposed to consult the corpse of her father on the matter. Are you there, father, said the Thief as he entered the darkened room, and Rin-dzin, in a sepulchral voice, replied, Ah - and to the question whether the Thief was his long-lost son, answered, You are.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Pretending urgent business that very night, the Thief made over the house and landed property to his 'sister' and took as his share a heavy bag of gold - leaving Rin-dzin behind. Borrowing a horse, Rin-dzin galloped after him and, dropping a new boot in the middle of the road and the fellow-boot further on, concealed himself; the Thief, finding one boot, thought it useless, and only at the second, nearly worn out, went back for the first - whereupon Rin-dzin emerged, picked up the bag of gold, strapped it to his saddle and rode on his way.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: Rice country with a great frontier river (symbolic pin in southern Tibet)
region.zh: 藏南有界河的產糧之地（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XIX

summary.en: A famine year sends the King of the Mice to the human King with a silk thread in place of a ceremonial scarf, to borrow a barnful of grain against the next harvest; hundreds of thousands of mice empty the barn in one night and repay with interest. When a richer enemy musters an army across the river, the Mouse-King asks for a hundred thousand foot-long sticks laid on the bank - and his subjects sail them across by night, gnawing bowstrings, musket-slimgs, fuses, pigtails and provisions until the camp wakes to find itself stripped and flees at the first bugle. The King builds the flood dam they ask for, bans cats on pain of death, and sends both kingdoms a yearly barnful in thanks.
summary.zh: 災年裡，鼠王手持一縷絲線（代替哈達）向人王借一倉糧，來年本利奉還；數十萬老鼠一夜搬空大倉，春季果然連本帶利償清。強敵陳兵界河對岸，鼠王討要十萬根一尺長的木棍沿河排列——當夜群鼠乘棍渡河，咬斷弓弦、火繩、背帶，啃碎衣袍髮辮與軍糧；敵營晨起大亂，一聲號角即全軍潰逃。國王依約築堤防洪、明令境內禁貓，並歲贈一倉糧以謝鼠功。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Mouse walked slowly up the Hall of Audience carrying in his hand a little silk thread instead of the usual ceremonial scarf, and petitioned for a barnful of grain on loan against the next harvest; that night hundreds of thousands of mice invaded the barn, each carrying off as much grain as he could in his mouth, on his back and curled up in his tail, until not a single grain of barley was left. In spring the loan was repaid with interest, and the King conceived a high opinion of their powers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: When a huge enemy army assembled across the frontier river, the King of the Mice asked only for one hundred thousand sticks, each about a foot long, laid in rows on the bank; at dusk his subjects launched the sticks on the river and embarked two or three at a time. In the sleeping camp each mouse began to do as much destruction as he possibly could - nibbling bowstrings and musket-slings, gnawing slow-matches and fuses, biting off clothes and pigtails - and after a couple of hours they sailed quietly home without having been detected.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: At daybreak every soldier found his clothes in rags, his pigtail cut off, his bow without a string, his rifle without a sling or fuse, and no provisions for breakfast; comrade quarrelled with comrade, and at the sound of bugles on the opposite bank the whole army took to flight. In accordance with the bargain the King built a strong embankment against floods and forbade all persons on pain of death to keep a cat within his frontiers - and every year thereafter sent the Mice a barnful of grain in thankful recognition of their services.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: Lakeside jungle in southern Tibet (symbolic pin in the lower Tsangpo gorge)
region.zh: 藏南雅魯藏布下游林澤（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XX

summary.en: A Monkey throws cocoanuts to a hungry Tortoise and hosts him in a cave for days; Mrs. Tortoise, jealous, summons her husband home with the physician's prescription of a Monkey's heart. Swimming the guest across the lake on his back, the Tortoise foolishly reveals the plot - and the Monkey, saying three or four hearts at least will be needed, gets set ashore, scales the tallest tree, and reviles his host. The Tortoise hides in their shared cave at dusk to ambush him; but the Monkey calls out 'Oh, great cave! great cave!' twice, hears no echo, muses aloud that the echo has vanished - and the foolish Tortoise, simulating it, betrays himself, while the Monkey chuckles and sleeps elsewhere.
summary.zh: 猴子擲椰果解龜之飢，並留他在山洞連宿數日；龜太太醋意大發，傳話「醫囑須用猴心為藥」。龜背猴渡湖時傻乎乎說破真相；猴子便稱「一顆猴心不夠，得三五顆」，騙得龜將他送回岸上，隨即上樹痛罵。入夜龜藏於二人同宿的岩洞設伏；猴到洞口連喊兩聲「大洞啊大洞！」不聞回聲，故意自語「奇怪，今晚怎麼沒有回聲」——蠢龜真的回了一聲「大洞啊大洞！」，猴子笑其愚蠢，到他處安睡。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The Monkey, watching the Tortoise's awkward attempts to climb a cocoanut-tree, broke off one or two cocoanuts and threw them down; the two struck up a friendship, the Monkey showed him a comfortable cave, and the Tortoise remained in the forest for several days. Mrs. Tortoise, not pleased that her husband amused himself with a vulgar Monkey, sent word that she was very ill, and that her physician had told her the only thing to cure her was a Monkey's heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Monkey mounted the Tortoise's back, and as they went across the lake the Tortoise foolishly let out that the only medicine to cure his wife was a Monkey's heart. The Monkey saw he was being led into a trap, and said that if she was as bad as all that one Monkey's heart would not be enough - three or four at least - and offered to fetch several friends; set ashore, he skipped up the tallest tree, reviling the Tortoise for inviting him to his home to kill him and use his heart as medicine for his ugly wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Tortoise hid in the darkest corner of their cave at dusk to catch the Monkey; but the Monkey came to the mouth and called out twice, Oh, great cave! great cave! - and, receiving no echo, remarked audibly that there used always to be an echo in this cave but he could not hear the slightest echo to-night. The foolish Tortoise, thinking that if he simulated an echo the Monkey would enter the cave as usual, gave answer from his dark corner - and the Monkey chuckled at the simplicity of the Tortoise and went off to sleep in some other part of the forest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: King Bacha of Room, the Queen on the Log, and the Boy Baki
title.zh: 魯姆王巴嘉、流放的王子與神童巴基

region.en: Country of Room, on a great river (symbolic pin; Room = the far-western lands of the tale world)
region.zh: 故事中的「魯姆國」大河之畔（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XXI

summary.en: Argumentative King Bacha bets his throne-side dignity on a fox being a tiger, and the politic council, preferring a king to a queen, rules for him - so the Queen is set adrift on a log. A magician on the far bank prophesies her a son, Baki, an incarnate Lama who walks and talks from birth; the neighboring king's huntsmen take them in, and Baki's pursuit of a snow-white doe whose skin falls away leads him into a cave kept by an Ogre, where a captured girl teaches him the mascot: a green Parrot on a red stone behind the sister rock - 'Great Raven, open the door.' The parrot's death drops the Ogre dead on his own threshold. Home again, Baki finds the King forcing marriage on his mother; as a cowrie-shell on the mounting-block he warns him, is smashed with a hammer, and each fragment becomes an armed demon who cuts the King to pieces - so the courtiers crown Baki, who marries the rescued girl.
summary.zh: 好辯的巴嘉王以「狐是虎」爭執不下；圓滑的大臣們寧可有王不可無王，裁定王勝——王后被縛上圓木順流放逐。對岸草原的老術士預言她將生下轉世喇嘛巴基，落地即能行走言語；鄰國王收留母子。巴基追一頭白母鹿入魔窟，被魔所囚的姑娘教他破魔之法：命繫於姊妹岩後紅石上的綠鸚鵡，三踢岩壁誦「大鴉，開門」。鸚鵡斃命，魔王橫死門檻。歸國後國王逼娶其母；巴基化螺螄伏於上馬石警告，被國王怒而錘碎——碎片化為持刀鬼卒，將國王剁成肉泥。眾臣擁立巴基為王，娶回姑娘；其母與巴嘉王和好，从此不再爭吵。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: The King maintained that the barking outside was a tiger and the Queen that it was a fox; the council, after the peasants confirmed no tiger came within many miles, privately agreed the King was in the wrong but publicly announced the opposite, lest they be left with only a Queen to reign over them. The poor Queen was taken down to the river and set astride a log of wood, floating down the great river many miles to the far bank.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: An old magician on the prairie prophesied that on a small hill a son would be born to her, the incarnation of a very holy Lama with miraculous qualities, able from birth to walk and talk, whose name was Baki. Pursuing a snow-white doe whose skin fell from her at the mouth of a cave, Baki was locked inside with a captured girl, who revealed the Ogre's secret: whatever damage you may do to his body is of no avail unless you can also destroy the object with which his spirit is bound up - a green Parrot on a red stone, reached by kicking the sister rock three times with the right foot, exclaiming at each kick, Great Raven, open the door.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Baki wrung the Parrot's neck and the Ogre lay dead across his own threshold; returning to the capital, he found the King had announced his intention of marrying Baki's mother. Transforming himself into a cowrie-shell on the King's mounting-block, he warned the King through the astonished groom that if he attempted to marry Prince Baki's mother he would find himself in a very unpleasant position - and when the furious King had a big hammer smash the shell, each piece turned into an armed man, Prince Baki among them, and the band of demons cut the King to pieces and vanished through the roof. The courtiers installed Baki as their new king.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Home-bred Boy: The Pig's Head, the Spiders and the Fly
title.zh: 家中寶貝兒：豬頭、蜘蛛與蒼蠅

region.en: Farmhouses and poplar groves of a Tibetan plateau (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 藏地高原農舍與楊樹林（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XXII

summary.en: Setting out at fifteen with horse, dog, gun and sword, the over-mothered Boy loses everything chasing a fox, and sleeps under a poplar where two Ravens gossip that his luck lies east. Beaten by a beggar and turned away from a wedding, he nests in the manure heap, kills a pig with a borrowed knife, and hides the head; when the lady's turquoise drops in the yard he covers it with a rag that a maid pockets into a wall-crevice, then presents himself as a famous magician whose enchanted pig's head detects thieves - having the rude bridegroom and the beggar thrashed and turned out, and the turquoise recovered from the crevice. Learning from the Ravens of a Spider family in a sick lady's ear, he simulates spring with green cloth, water and drum-thunder, wraps up the seven spiders as they emerge, and is rewarded again; challenged at sword-point by the vengeful beggar to name what he holds in his fist, the Boy answers that he is as much in his power as the fly - and the superstitious old man becomes his admirer and leads him to his recovered horse and dog.
summary.zh: 十五歲少年初次出門，追狐而失馬、犬、槍、刀，夜宿楊樹下偷聽鴉語「向東方去自有福」。受乞兒辱打、被婚宴逐出後，他睡進糞堆，借刀殺豬藏頭；貴婦綠松石落在院中，他以破布蓋之，被侍女連布拾起塞入牆縫。他自稱法師，持「神豬頭」驗賊——無禮的新郎與乞兒挨打逐出，綠松石自牆縫尋回。再聽鴉語得知貴婦耳中藏蛛，他鋪綠布、灑水、擊鼓作「春雷」，七隻蜘蛛盡出被裹殺。懷恨的乞兒持刀逼他猜左拳中之物，他嘆道「我如你掌中之蠅任你捏殺」——老乞兒誤以為神通，反成其崇拜者，領他尋回馬與犬。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: Chasing a fox that darted out with the Boy's hat sticking over its head, he lost horse, dog, gun, sword and outer robe; under a poplar two Ravens gossiped at dawn that a foolish home-bred Boy had lost everything and that he had only to go towards the villages which lie towards the east. Beaten by a mocking Beggar and driven from a wedding feast as an ill-omened creature, he dug a nest in a manure heap, borrowed a knife on the plea of cutting dry meat, killed one of the pigs, and hid the head with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: A large and valuable turquoise fell from the Lady's headdress in the yard; afraid to leave his nest, the Boy threw a piece of rag over it, and a maid picked up rag and turquoise together and thrust them into a crevice in the wall. When all the famous diviners, magicians and lamas of the neighbourhood had failed, the Boy presented himself as a famous magician, walked round with the pig's head under his arm, and had the rude Bridegroom and the insulting Beggar thrashed and turned out as the head grew agitated before each - and the turquoise was found inside the rag in the crevice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the Ravens he learned that the pain in a sick Lady's ear came from a Spider family lodged in her head, to be dislodged only by making them believe spring had come: green cloth spread and sprinkled with water would look like a wet spring field, and a drum beaten to simulate thunder would bring them out. The old Mother Spider came down to test the water and climbed back with the good news; at the drums the whole family, seven in number, let themselves down onto the green cloth and were wrapped up and destroyed - and the Lady overwhelmed the Boy with gifts. Challenged by the vengeful old Beggar to say what he held in his left fist or die by the sword, the Boy replied that he was as much in his power as the fly he held - and the old man, taking it for a proof of supernatural powers, became his ardent admirer and led him to the valley where his horse and dog were found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Home-bred Boy Defeats the Enemy

region.en: Enemy camp below a reconnaissance hill (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 偵察山坡下之敵營（象徵定位）

texts.period: Collected and translated by W. F. O'Connor, 1906

source.work: W. F. O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet, London 1906, Story XXII (final part)

summary.en: Famous for magic, the home-bred Boy is asked by his King to aid the war effort and dares not refuse a magnificent charger he cannot ride; his servant ties his feet under the horse's belly. At the first trumpet the horse bolts straight for the enemy camp; seizing a dead tree-branch to check it, he is carried in with the branch in his hands, hair loose, shouting at his horse - and the enemy, never having seen such a terrific-looking object, take him for a demon and a threat of annihilation. Offering silken scarfs, the General and his officers beg peace on condition they can stop the horse - and the Boy formally accepts their surrender and dictates terms.
summary.zh: 少年以「神通」聞名，國王請他出征，他不敢推辭駿馬卻不會騎——僕人以繩縛其雙足於馬腹下。一聲號角，戰馬直衝敵營；他抓住枯枝想勒馬，卻被連枝帶入敵陣，散髮狂喊。敵軍從未見過這等「魔物」，以為惡魔降臨滅頂在即，紛紛獻哈達求和；他趁勢開出條件——你們得先勒住我的馬——將軍與眾官兩側拽韁，他遂正式受降、口授和約。

sensitivity.note: Folk tales collected 1906; treated respectfully as Tibetan heritage.

passages.text: In reality a very bad rider, the Boy had his servant tie his feet together with a rope under the horse's belly; at the sound of a trumpet the frightened horse dashed off down the hill at full gallop straight towards the enemy's camp. Just before reaching it the horse carried him under a dead tree, the rotten bough broke in his grasp as he seized it, and he was swept into the camp holding a huge branch of the tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hither and thither rushed the horse amongst the tents, trampling the frightened soldiers underfoot, while the Boy swept his great branch to and fro; his hair flew wildly, his shouts increased the terror of his appearance, and the soldiers, never having seen such a terrific-looking object, concluded he must be a demon attacking them, and instead of opposing tried to soothe him with silken scarfs. The General and the principal officers coming out in a body begged peace, and the Boy, unable to control his horse, shouted that he accepted their submission on condition that they were able to stop it; they seized the bridle on either side, and he formally accepted their surrender and dictated terms of peace. The King raised him to the highest rank with lands and gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of O'Connor, Folk Tales from Tibet (1906); not verbatim.
